claims.text: A machine-learning framework can optimize thermomechanical processing parameters to provide deterministic control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The initial Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy has a multiphase or incipient-multiphase microstructure.
Existing processing–microstructure datasets can be used to determine optimized heat-treatment protocols for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
Annealing, solution treatment, and controlled cooling can be tailored by the proposed model to control the alloy's phase evolution.
Optimized processing conditions can modulate phase nucleation and growth kinetics.
Processing changes can alter the relative fractions and distributions of phases in a high-entropy alloy.
FCC and B2 are among the phases whose fractions or distributions may be controlled in the proposed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy.
A machine-learning model can correlate historical processing parameters with resulting microstructures.
Those correlations can predict thermomechanical conditions that favor or suppress specific phases.
Machine-learning-guided processing can control nucleation and growth barriers.
Predictive processing control can overcome the trial-and-error limitations of classical heat treatment.
Machine-learning-guided processing will produce a more reproducible and targeted phase distribution than conventional fixed-parameter processing.
A targeted phase distribution will enhance mechanical or other functional properties.
Traditional fixed-parameter and trial-and-error heat treatments yield variable, less controllable multiphase microstructures.
The effectiveness of the proposed method depends on the quality and coverage of the historical training data.
Variations in processing conditions, equipment, and sample geometry may affect the resulting phase evolution.
XRD can be used for phase identification, while SEM and TEM can be used for microstructural assessment.
Hardness and compressive-strength testing can assess mechanical performance associated with processing and microstructure.
